EDM Might Be the Way Drilling a hole sounds simple, until you need to do it with extreme precision, into hardened materials, or to microscopic depths. That’s when you start comparing EDM hole drilling and conventional CNC drilling side by side. While both are designed to create holes, their technologies, capabilities, and ideal use cases couldn’t be more different. So, which method should you choose for your next project? Let’s dig in. What Is EDM Hole Drilling? EDM (Electrical Discharge Machining) hole drilling , also called hole popping EDM or EDM deep hole drilling , uses electrical sparks to erode material. Instead of a rotating drill bit, it uses a tubular electrode and dielectric fluid to remove metal through high-frequency discharges. It’s a non-contact process, meaning the tool doesn’t make direct physical contact with the material during machining. The result? It can drill extremely precise, burr-free holes even in hardened steel, carbides, or exotic alloys . What Is Conventional CNC Hole Drilling? CNC hole drilling uses rotating cutting tools<dynamic-value> twist drills or end mills, to cut into material. It's what most people imagine when they think about machining a hole. From high-speed spindles to peck drilling cycles, CNC machines are versatile and fast, especially when you're working with softer materials or mass production. But it’s still a contact-based process , and precision can degrade with wear, heat, or vibration. EDM vs Drilling: The Core Differences Feature EDM Hole Drilling CNC Drilling Material Type Conductive materials only (e.g., steel, titanium) Any machinable material Tool Contact No physical contact Direct contact via tool Hole Size Micro to medium (0.1 mm to 6 mm) Wide range (0.5 mm to 50+ mm) Tolerance Extremely tight (±0.002 mm possible) Moderate (±0.05 mm typical) Hole Depth Excellent for deep, narrow holes (30:1+ depth-to-diameter) Limited by tool rigidity and chip evacuation Speed Slower Faster for larger holes Surface Finish Very smooth, no burrs May require deburring or finishing Tool Wear Minimal due to no mechanical contact High, especially in hard materials Are you unsure about which process is right for your metal part? We can help you choose the most precise and cost-effective method for your job. Get a free quote here and let's make your design manufacturable. When to Use EDM Hole Drilling The EDM hole drilling process shines in high-precision, small-diameter, deep-hole situations, especially where conventional drilling fails or causes tool breakage. Use cases include: ● Turbine blades (for cooling holes) ● Fuel injector nozzles ● Aerospace components ● Medical devices requiring micro holes ● Hard tool steels or materials like Inconel and titanium Also, EDM is ideal when you need starter holes for wire EDM , which conventional tools can’t drill due to hardness or geometry. When to Use Conventional CNC Drilling For general-purpose hole making in aluminum, plastics, or mild steel, CNC hole drilling is faster and more cost-effective. Use cases include: ● Bolt holes, pilot holes, tapped holes ● Large hole drilling in brackets or frames ● Machining production parts in batches ● Applications where tight tolerance is not critical And yes, to answer a common question, can a CNC machine drill holes? Absolutely. In fact, it’s one of the most common operations in any CNC shop. EDM Holes vs Drilled Holes: What About Quality? EDM holes tend to be cleaner and burr-free straight off the machine. Their surface finish is smoother, with no mechanical stress or deformation around the hole. This makes them ideal for critical applications where dimensional stability and fatigue resistance matter. CNC-drilled holes, on the other hand, often need secondary processes , like deburring or reaming, to meet similar tolerances and finishes, especially in small diameters or deep holes. Limitations to Consider While EDM hole drilling offers unmatched precision, it’s not ideal for every scenario . ● It can’t be used on non-conductive materials (like plastic or glass). ● It’s relatively slow for large-diameter holes. ● Machines and electrodes are more expensive and require specialized operators. Conversely, CNC drilling tools wear faster in hardened materials, and the deeper you go, the higher the risk of tool deflection, chatter, or breakage . EDM Hole Drilling Machines: What Makes Them Special? A dedicated hole drilling EDM machine is typically compact, automated, and capable of producing holes as small as 0.1 mm in tough metals. Many come with automatic electrode changers and multi-axis positioning. For shops working with aerospace, mold making, or die sinking, having one on the floor is a game-changer for precision parts. Want Extreme Accuracy? EDM Might Be the Way If you're prototyping intricate components or producing parts where one imperfect hole can ruin the entire build , go for EDM. But if you’re running production batches, drilling aluminum brackets, or cutting costs, CNC drilling is often more practical. Choose the Right Tool for the Hole Not every hole is created equal, and neither are the tools that make them. Whether you choose EDM hole drilling for ultra-precision or CNC hole drilling for speed and efficiency, understanding their strengths is the first step toward better manufacturing outcomes. If you’re unsure what your application calls for, talk to your machinist, or even better, partner with a shop that offers both options .
